rv.q: When you reach the end of “Anarchist,” you may feel you’ve traveled an unnecessarily winding road to get there.
Mamet is slow and stingy in dispensing details, maybe in an attempt to make the encounter a pure philosophical debate.

Yet you just cannot help but see "The Anarchist" as a cautionary tale for the writer who gains so much clout that he can now get anything up in the great American marketplace without any of the usual formative niceties, without any of the usual checks and balances.
It is hard not to wish he were as interested in it as a play.
For all the skill with which Ms. Peet has constructed her play, it remains stubbornly static.
No one talks like this and the two actresses struggle to make something unnatural seem natural.
But he can’t seriously expect Broadway auds to share his fascination with the 1960s radical politics of the Weathermen, which he explores ad nauseam in “The Anarchist.”

Despite a career-long crusade to streamline theater by sandblasting away its airy effeminacies (like acting and emoting), his latest, The Anarchist, still feels strangely gassy, even at a Spanxed 80 minutes.

But the far greater problem with The Anarchist is that this aridly intellectual two-hander — which clocks in at a mere 65 minutes and has been loftily described by Mamet as "a Talmudic argument" — is desiccated, dull and virtually without drama.
Certainly, The Anarchist leaves no shortage of material for after-theater debate.
David Mamet's new play The Anarchist is not so much a drama about specific people in a narrative arc as a short, brittle, stripped-down debate-club exercise on a stopwatch.
If you ask me, I'm still glad to have been part of the mob who demanded an original drama, but The Anarchist could have used a lot more blood and tears.
If only the same could be said of Mamet's play.
'The Anarchist' only runs 65 minutes, but I doubt there'll be any complaints that it's too short.
Even at just 70 intermissionless minutes, 'The Anarchist' is a challenge to sentience.
Mamet certainly believes in punishing his audience.

cn.t: Mamet's 70-minute two-hander earns widespread criticism as inert, pretentious, and dramatically static despite strong performances from LuPone and Winger, with most reviewers finding the philosophical debate dry and interminable.

vs.sum: The John Golden Theatre offers good sightlines from most seats, though sound quality can vary, especially under the mezzanine. Seating comfort is typical of older theaters with tight legroom, but the venue maintains a pleasant ambiance overall. Facilities are adequate, though not exceptional.

acc.note: 5 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No wheelchair-accessible restroom (use adjacent Schoenfeld).
